articles.title: Hemos tenido que esperar mucho, sí, pero 'GTA 6' es una auténtica locura
articles.text:
El vistazo extendido a GTA 6 que ya se puede ver en Netflix, y que en cuestión de horas estará disponible en YouTube, es la prueba cabal de que la espera por el juego ha sido tediosa e insoportable por momentos, pero que ha valido la pena. Es lógico pensar que ningún fanático de la saga Grand Theft Auto ha quedado insatisfecho tras los 26 minutos de material que ha liberado Rockstar Games.
Sí, el enfado por lanzar el vistazo extendido a GTA 6 en Netflix es comprensible y compartido. Sin embargo, es una realidad que muchos han optado por verlo en otras plataformas aprovechando la apertura a las reacciones de streamers y creadores de contenido. Lo gracioso es que algunos de estos han quedado tan boquiabiertos con el avance que han emitido el mínimo posible de comentarios e interrupciones.
Otro punto interesante es que tras el lanzamiento de esta mirada extendida a GTA 6, parece que Rockstar ha podido dar vuelta la página tras las filtraciones de Cyberleek. El material que se ha presentado es alucinante y está muy bien pulido, incluso para ser un juego que el propio estudio ha reconocido que aún no está terminado.
Por supuesto que la empresa ha elegido qué mostrar y qué no, pero lo que se ha podido ver es lisa y llanamente formidable. Vale mencionar que tanto las cinemáticas como el gameplay se han capturado con una PS5, siguiendo con lo ya visto en los tráilers anteriores. Además, los responsables del juego han ratificado que se lanzará el próximo 19 de noviembre.
Lo que ha revelado el vistazo en profundidad a GTA 6
Tal y como se esperaba, el detalle a nivel de gráficos e interacciones de GTA 6 es espectacular. El vistazo extendido ha revelado varios puntos importantes de la historia y la relación entre Jason y Lucía, los protagonistas, pero también ha permitido ver una gran variedad de minijuegos y actividades en paralelo a las misiones principales.
Así, se ha mostrado a los personajes practicando baloncesto, participando de carreras de coches y motocross, paseando en motos de agua y lanchas, visitando clubes de desnudistas y entrenando en el gimnasio. En una de las últimas escenas mostradas incluso se ve a Lucía lanzándose en paracaídas desde la azotea de un edificio.
Respecto del gameplay, GTA 6 no defrauda. En el vistazo extendido se observan escenas de acción impactantes, con tiroteos en una cocina de droga y múltiples persecuciones de alto octanaje. En este último apartado se aprecian dinámicas muy interesantes al poder abordar las escenas desde dos puntos de vista diferentes.
Así, por ejemplo, durante una persecución habrá que controlar a Jason cuando dispare contra coches de la policía mientras cuelga de la ventana del auto de escape, con Lucía al volante. En tanto que en otros fragmentos habrá que controlar el vehículo, mientras los NPC llevan adelante la balacera. También hay lugar para la sátira y la burla, algo que se ha visto especialmente en una escena en la que Lucía escapa con un auto robado, mientras un influencer en el maletero continúa transmitiendo todo en directo desde su móvil.
Una espera que ha valido la pena
El combate cuerpo a cuerpo también promete un control bastante granular en GTA 6, con una dinámica que reparte las acciones de una misma misión entre los dos protagonistas. Rockstar también le ha dedicado mucho tiempo a pulir el control de las armas, pudiendo esconderlas antes de concretar un atraco, o, incluso, manejar escopetas con una sola mano, mientras se lleva carga importante en la otra.
El sistema de calificación de "buscado" cuenta con seis estrellas, dependiendo de la severidad de los delitos que se cometan. Además, según qué acciones se concreten, los protagonistas muestran tanto una barra de resistencia como una de enfoque. Y las decisiones que tomen no solo van a impactar en el desenlace de la misión, sino también en su apariencia e integridad física.
Esto es apenas una pizca de lo que ha reflejado el vistazo en profundidad a GTA 6. Lo nuevo de Rockstar Games lo tiene todo para ser una experiencia realmente alucinante y este material deja en claro que la espera no fue en vano.

articles.title: YouTube now lets creators tag Amazon products and earn commissions from purchases | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube announced on Thursday that eligible creators in the U.S. can now tag Amazon products in their content and receive a cut of sales. Creators can link Amazon products in their shorts, long-form videos, and livestreams.
The update turns product recommendations into a more direct revenue stream for creators, and for Amazon, the move puts its massive online marketplace inside one of the most popular video platforms.
Although YouTube already runs a Shopping affiliate program with participating retailers, the addition of Amazon’s vast catalog essentially allows creators to recommend a variety of products through a native integration. By bringing Amazon into the Shopping Affiliate Program, creators no longer need to paste Associates links in the video’s description, then hope viewers copy the link when they make a purchase.
Instead, YouTube says Amazon will provide it with a curated catalog of highly requested and trending products that creators can tag in their videos. If a creator can’t find a specific product that they want to tag, they can request to add it by reaching out to YouTube Support.
The feature also includes auto-tagging support. If enabled, YouTube’s systems can automatically review a creator’s recent uploads to identify and tag eligible Amazon products.
YouTube notes that creators won’t see breakdowns for specific products or individual videos in their analytics, but that they’ll see their overall daily earnings in YouTube Studio. If a viewer ends up returning an item, that commission will be deducted from the creator’s balance.
While only eligible U.S. creators can currently tag Amazon products, those tags can be seen globally. YouTube says it may automatically match a tagged product with a trusted local merchant offer to allow creators to earn commissions on eligible international purchases. If a local merchant isn’t available, the tag will route viewers to the Amazon U.S. website, where commission will be earned if a purchase is finalized on the U.S. site.
To be eligible, creators must be enrolled in YouTube’s Partner and Shopping Affiliate programs, have an active Amazon Influencer or Associates account, and link it to their YouTube channel.

articles.title: From Spec To Formal Properties
articles.text:
Can LLMs turn a specification into a set of formal properties that can be used to verify an implementation? The answer is getting closer to being yes, but with caveats.
Key Takeaways:
One of the biggest problems for formal verification has always been the difficulty associated with writing properties. While language standards have been in place for a couple of decades and tools have improved dramatically, that roadblock has never been cleared — perhaps until now, thanks to AI.
AI is known for its ability to read a natural language document and synthesize information from it. One application with high utility would be the ability to read a specification and to automatically create a set of properties that could be used to verify if an implementation matches the specification.
However, several challenges exist, and a number of pitfalls await those who do not fully understand the hazards.
One portion of the SystemVerilog language enables properties of a design to be formally defined. When these properties are used within a verification environment, they are referred to as assertions. Properties define logical and temporal relationships between signals, enabling protocols and other things to be explicitly defined. A set of properties should be able to define the complete set of behaviors intended in a design and to do that without being entangled with how those behaviors are realized. In that respect, they represent a specification against which an RTL implementation can be judged for correctness.
But the SystemVerilogAssertion (SVA) language is not easy to learn, especially given that it is declarative in nature, rather than the object-oriented procedural nature of languages used in most parts of the design and verification flow. For many years, the industry has attempted to create tools and methodologies that make their creation simpler. Recently, LLM-based tools have started to make significant headway even though there are several breakthroughs that still need to be made.
One recent breakthrough is the creation of knowledge graphs, which are defined by Cohen and Chibani [1]. “A knowledge graph stores information as a network of things and the relationships between them, rather than as flat text. It has three parts: nodes (the entities — a signal, a module, a requirement, a port); edges (the relationships — drives, resets, responds-to, belongs-to); and triples, the storage unit, written as (subject → relationship → object).”
KGs act as a database of information that can be quickly accessed, rather than relying on the LLM to extract it every time it’s needed. “Ordinary RAG retrieves chunks of text that look relevant; a KG retrieves specific facts and their connections. That is why the KG-based frameworks argue they give better grounding — there is less chance the model invents a signal name or misreads a relationship, because the relationships are stored explicitly. [1]”
Ironically, one big problem is finding an adequate specification. “The ideal is that you have a perfect spec, but that has not existed at least in the last 30 years,” says Ravindra Aneja, director of applications engineering at Synopsys. “The majority of the time there will not be a perfect spec. In fact, you may not have any spec at all. This may depend on whether it is a new design or a derivative design, who is writing it, and which organization. But until AI came along, the notion of having a perfect spec or documentation was not the coolest thing to do in the world. People often start designing before they fill in the spec because they already have some ideas about what they want to do. With the advent of AI, people are paying more attention.”
A significant amount can be accomplished today. “AI can read a spec document, a protocol standard, or even RTL comments and propose a first pass of assertions covering resets, handshakes, one-hot conditions, and obvious safety checks,” says Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “This is possible when the specifications are on standards that do not change frequently. That draft speeds up the tedious part of writing boilerplate SVA.”
The desire to do this has existed for some time. “People claim that reading a specification and converting it into some other tangible artifact is something that AI is well suited to solve,” says Abhi Kolpekwa, senior vice-president and general manager at Siemens EDA. “It also needs an aspect of change management, because the spec is likely to change. For a verification flow to have change management, there is a lot more that needs to happen outside of agents. This is called contextual intelligence. We need the ability to create a context and contextual intelligence that not only understands the changes, but also makes more informed decisions considering the history and a possible future in the given verification flow context.”
Specifications are never fixed. “I’m in the process of figuring out the spec and I’m doing the development, but marketing then wants this additional feature, and you go back and modify the spec,” says Synopsys’ Aneja. “Sometimes that deviation could be minor. Sometimes it could be major. Whatever changes you are making, how would it reflect in your design and in your verification environment? AI is pretty good at this, figuring out what the deviation is and how it is going to impact your verification. There’s a lot of discussion in the industry about how you can manage this change-based design process. This is where AI is going to be very useful.”
Danger ahead
Was that specification complete? “Completeness is a different question entirely,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “Most real-life silicon development does not happen in isolation. And even when projects are entirely new, it is rare that complete specifications would be written capturing all micro-architecture and architecture, including interfaces where typically most bugs reside. In my experience, AI-generated property sets are strong on structural and syntactic coverage and weak on architectural intent, and the ‘why’ behind a rule. So usefulness is real, but completeness has to be established independently, usually by an engineer who understands the design intent well enough to know what is missing.”
Was all information used? “How useful and complete those assertions are depends on how good your AI engine is, and how accurately it understands the nuances of the specifications,” says Yaron Ilani, design verification solutions engineer at Normal Computing. “At Normal, we tackle this challenge by running ‘auto formalization’ and generating an ontology. The risks could be wrong assumptions resulting from gaps or ambiguity in the specifications. These risks could be mitigated by running a preliminary step of spec auditing.”
Both problems can result in an incomplete set of properties. “The biggest danger is false confidence,” says Darbari. “A team gets a large batch of properties, runs them through a formal tool, sees green proofs, and treats that as sign-off. But a proof is only as good as the property, and a weak or vacuous property proves trivially without checking anything meaningful. AI-generated properties are particularly prone to this because a model can produce syntactically valid SVA that is logically too permissive, missing or over-constraining an antecedent, or checking the wrong signal relationship — and it will still compile and pass.”
That ends up being a verification task itself. “Deriving properties from a spec requires distilling unstructured and multimodal information into provable statements,” says Hanna Yip, product manager lead at Normal. “While the extraction process itself can be efficient, it can be quite challenging to ensure what’s extracted is correct.”
In the past, verification happened when the design team interpreted the specification, the verification team interpreted the specification, and then those interpretations were verified against each other. Sometimes that identified a problem with the specification itself. “Generated properties can quietly encode the AI’s own misreading of the spec as if it were ground truth,” says Darbari. “Errors in interpretation get baked into what looks like a rigorous artifact. There is also a scale risk. If these properties feed downstream FMEDA, safety cases, or certification evidence for ISO 26262 or ISO 21434, an unnoticed gap does not stay contained to one project.”
It quietly means that you cannot trust what AI has done. “Trust is a big issue,” says Kaye Mao, product design lead at Normal. “How do you verify work that you did not do, especially when agents are hyper-confident in their correctness and trained to pass the sniff test? For example, how do you verify a test is actually testing the design as outlined in the spec? Do you have to look at the actual waveforms? That itself is time-consuming, so it may require novel ways of checking agent work.”
Given recent incidents with AI going rogue, Mao adds another potential concern. “Another danger is failing to limit what collateral the agent can access for a given task. Agents will always cheat if possible. For example, they may use the design to generate test cases, which defeats the point of keeping verification and design separate.”
ROI
While it is clear that AI is capable of doing some aspects of the task, it also has costs and creates new work. Does it add up to a significant gain? “I’m increasingly noticing that silicon design houses — even the ones who are building AI hardware powering the agents — are getting nervous about unreasonable use of agentic AI in particular by junior engineers and people who are quick to claim they are experts without the hands-on experience,” says Darbari. “It is efficient at the front end, but it can be inefficient at the back end if teams are not careful.”
This may improve over time. “It depends on how big the spec is,” says Normal’s Kao. “More philosophically, if we define efficiency as saving engineers time, it’s unclear, given the new tasks of verifying agent output, how much actual engineering-time efficiency we see today. I expect efficiency gains to improve as models get better and we devise better ways of verifying agent work.”
There are several ways this can be measured. “Complexity scaling is not strictly computational,” says Arvind Srinivasan, head of solution architect at Normal. “There’s a human efficiency associated with data completeness and review. As with handwritten properties, simple, well-documented parts of a spec are easier to cover than more sophisticated parts of the design. To enable sublinear scaling of formal coverage in modern designs, there is a need to augment existing formal tooling with AI-native formal tooling and alternative, non-SVA autoformalization strategies.”
Scaling has always been an important aspect when formal solvers are used. “There are a lot of techniques in the formal world, which helps you scale,” says Aneja. “The good news is that in the past we had to train junior engineers about these techniques. Now you can provide that knowledge base within these agents, and when they write the property, they can become very efficient in writing those formal properties. That will give you better answers, much faster answers. You’ll be able to do more in the same amount of time. It helps you in scalability.”
Human in the loop
All agentic flows need a human in the loop today. “Drafting hundreds of candidate properties that used to take days of manual reading now takes minutes, and that is a genuine productivity gain,” says Darbari. “Where the efficiency can evaporate is in review. If every generated property or debug waveform needs the same depth of scrutiny as a manually generated one, and the volume has gone up tenfold, the review burden can outpace the drafting savings.”
Someone has to review it. “You can’t just take it as it is because otherwise you’ll be shooting yourself in the foot,” says Aneja. “LLMs can do a lot of interesting stuff, but they can also fool you. That’s the reality of life. It can give you a lot of automation, provide a lot of efficiency and productivity, but someone who knows that design will have to review it manually, tweak it, guide it, and you keep accumulating that information. Over time, you may be able to train it or get to a point where it can do a pretty reasonable job out of the box.”
There are many ways that LLMs can fool you. “Vacuity checking, coverage analysis, and cross-checking against the spec still have to happen, and those steps do not get faster just because generation did,” says Darbari. “They should run vacuity and coverage checks as standard practice, not as an afterthought, because generated sets are more likely to contain trivially true properties than carefully hand-crafted ones.”
But this still creates a problem. “People want to stay in control, because they’re held accountable for the consequences,” says Mao. “It seems unrealistic to expect folks to understand formal. Rather, what other representations can be used to verify the accuracy of a formal representation of a spec? Is it waveforms? Is it something else?”
Standard practices need to be built into the flow. “Treat AI-generated properties as a draft, never as an accepted deliverable,” recommends Darbari. “Build a review gate into the flow before anything reaches a regression suite. Users should insist on provenance — which spec section, which requirement, or which RTL construct produced each property — so reviewers can trace back and check the mapping.”
If trust is built, the gains get larger. “This is good news for DV engineers looking to get into formal verification or assertion-based simulation,” says Normal’s Ilani. “For many years, we used to joke that writing effective formal properties requires a PhD. Now, AI-driven flows lower the barrier to entry for DV engineers looking to run formal verification. Part of this new methodology, in my opinion, is to leverage agentic flows and make them your wingman, your PhD in formal verification assistant, to help you not only understand your formal testbench, but also run it, debug failures, and propose solutions.”
Reference
1. RAG-SVA in the Landscape of LLM-Based Assertion Generation, Cohen and Chibani
[Editor’s Note. Part two will dig deeper into the team skills required and the best ways to introduce those into a methodology. It will explore whether this will enable raising the level of abstraction.]

articles.title: Tech Solutions for Secure & Smart Home Storage - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Managing household items gets tricky when closets overflow, and garages fill up fast. Technology gives modern homeowners better choices to organize, track, and guard their belongings.
Upgrading home spaces with digital tools creates order out of daily clutter. Smart setups protect valuable gear and keep everyday items within easy reach.
Smart Sensors and Inventory Tracking Tools
Modern setups use small sensors attached to shelves and storage bins. These tiny devices track item movements and send updates directly to mobile devices. Users receive notification alerts when items get moved or removed from designated shelves.
Inventory tracking becomes especially useful when belongings are kept in an off-site storage unit. People who find self storage facilities in Brisbane can use digital tracking tools to maintain a record of boxes, furniture, equipment, or business stock stored outside the home. This makes it easier to know what is in storage without opening every container or making unnecessary trips to the facility.
Bluetooth beacons make locating specific bins in dark basements fast and easy. Users open a phone app to trigger visual light cues or chime sounds on attached tags. Searching through dozens of identical cardboard containers becomes a quick digital task.
Sensors monitor weight changes inside storage bins to track supply quantities. When household items run low, automated lists prompt owners to restock supplies. Smart tracking prevents surprise shortages of everyday goods.
Automated Storage and IoT Solutions
Advanced modern storage replaces manual organization with connected hardware and data tools. Unlike older methods, smart storage relies on automated systems, data analytics, and IoT tech to maximize space, cut human error, and speed up retrieval times. Automated systems adjust storage racks based on usage frequency.
Connected hubs sync storage activity across multiple rooms in real time. People can locate stored boxes in seconds using simple mobile dashboard views. Central systems log every entry and item transfer across home storage networks.
Data analytics predict seasonal storage needs based on historical usage patterns. The system suggests moving winter gear to accessible front shelves as temperatures drop. Smart scheduling keeps relevant gear at arm’s length throughout the year.
Smart storage networks connect directly with home automation platforms to streamline daily routines. Custom automation rules trigger cabinet lights when motion detectors sense someone approaching. Integrated setups transform standard storage rooms into responsive utility spaces.
- Automated shelf adjusters for heavy bins
- IoT temperature trackers for delicate goods
- Digital labels with instant scanning capability
Keyless Access and Digital Lock Technologies
Physical metal keys disappear quickly inside crowded drawers. Modern locks replace physical brass keys with numeric keypads, mobile apps, or biometric scanners. Fingerprint sensors unlock storage cabinets in under one second.
PIN codes let family members open secure lockers without carrying extra keys around. Temporary guest passes grant short access to visitors when needed. Master users revoke shared digital keys instantly through a central mobile app interface.
Activity logs display exact times when cabinet doors open or shut. Homeowners receive immediate notifications whenever unauthorized code attempts happen. Built-in tamper alarms sound loudly if anyone tries forcing lock mechanisms open.
Biometric locks offer individual profile settings for different family members. Parents restrict access to dangerous power tools or chemical cleaning supplies. Custom permission levels keep household storage safe for children.
Climate-Controlled Smart Cabinets
Electronics, paper records, and expensive fabrics spoil quickly when moisture builds up inside storage areas. Connected climate cabinets maintain steady temperature levels automatically. Internal sensors adjust heating and cooling elements to protect sensitive belongings.
Built-in humidity monitors adjust airflow whenever room moisture shifts upwards. Internal fans activate silently to prevent mold growth on delicate collectibles and artwork. Sealed gaskets keep ambient outdoor air from leaking inside cabinet enclosures.
Notifications send warning alerts directly to phones if power failures occur. Owners fix environmental problems before sensitive gear suffers permanent damage. Backup battery units maintain internal climate settings during temporary power grid drops.
Dehumidifiers integrate directly with smart home control panels for distant monitoring. Historical logs display daily humidity and temperature charts over long periods. Property owners track climate stability across seasonal weather changes.
Automated Vertical Storage Systems
High ceilings hold unused space in garages, closets, and utility rooms. Motorized overhead racks bring high storage bins down with simple wall button controls. Motorized lifts eliminate dangerous climbs up stepladders to retrieve top boxes.
Ceiling mounts hold heavy seasonal gear high above vehicle parking zones. Automatic safety sensors stop moving racks if objects block lower paths below. Weight limits trigger automatic safety cutoffs to prevent motor strains.
Smart vertical shelves adjust height settings based on container dimensions. High-density storage modules stack items tightly to clear valuable floor space. Compact designs double usable storage volume without expanding room footprints.
Heavy-duty electric motors raise kayak racks, bike lifts, and tire stacks smoothly. Wireless remote controls allow operation from anywhere inside the garage space. Vertical organization turns cluttered floors into usable workspace.
- Motorized ceiling hoists for bulky boxes
- Drop-down wall shelves for high closet spots
- Weight sensors to prevent mechanical overloading
Cloud Integrated Home Inventory Apps
Keeping track of stored belongings takes time without proper documentation. Digital inventory applications let users snap photos of box contents before sealing lids. High-resolution images save alongside custom descriptions and purchase receipt scans.
Search functions pinpoint exact bin numbers for specific household items. Category tags help organize holiday decorations, spare tools, and old documents seamlessly. Color-coded tag systems group items by room location or usage frequency.
Digital records make insurance claims simpler if property damage happens unexpectedly. Detailed photo logs prove asset value without manual paperwork searches. Cloud backups store inventory data safely away from physical hardware destruction.
Barcodes and QR code stickers stick onto container sides for rapid scanning. Scanning a code with a smartphone camera reveals full box contents without opening tape seals. Digital cataloging speeds up moving processes and seasonal item retrieval.
Security Camera Integration for Storage Spaces
Monitoring storage areas protects valuable goods from theft and damage. Compact security cameras cover blind spots inside dark sheds, attics, and basements. Infrared lenses capture clear video footage even in complete darkness.
Motion detection sensors activate camera feeds only when movement occurs. System alerts push live video streams directly to smartphone lock screens. Cloud storage saves motion events securely for immediate review.
Microphones allow two-way audio communication around detached garage areas. Remote viewing lets owners monitor property safety from anywhere instantly. Integrated spotlights illuminate dark storage zones when motion sensors trigger.
AI camera software distinguishes family members from unknown intruders automatically. Smart filters prevent false alarms caused by pets or passing outdoor wildlife. Constant monitoring keeps high-value stored items safe around the clock.
Modern technology transforms household storage into secure, organized space. Smart hardware, mobile tools, and automated racks keep personal property safe and easy to reach.
Simple digital upgrades help homeowners maintain clear living areas year-round. Investing in smart storage brings long-term order, convenience, and peace of mind.

articles.title: Nigeria’s SecVite helps organisers manage events end-to-end from their phone - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup SecVite is a mobile-first platform for managing events from start to finish, and the platform is already seeing strong traction.
Launched last October by founder Hameed Yusuf, SecVite allows users to create an event; invite and manage guests; handle RSVPs and approvals; sell tickets; collect payments, gifts and contributions; and check guests in using QR codes.
“We started with private celebrations like weddings, but the platform can also be used for birthdays, conferences and other events,” Yusuf told Disrupt Africa.
The idea for SecVite, in fact, came from planning his own wedding.
“I had hundreds of guests to manage and I was personally handling things like guest approvals and invitations. At some point I realised there had to be a better way to do it,” he said.
A senior software engineer with over 10 years of experience, Yusuf started building a solution himself, and used his wedding as the first real test.
“We managed more than 400 guests through SecVite, and over 300 guests were checked in using QR codes,” he said. “That was important because it meant we were not just building something in theory. We had actually used it in a real event with hundreds of people.”
He then formally launched SecVite, a platform he said differentiates itself by its end-to-end nature and the fact it works for different types of events.
“What stood out to me was how many different tools people use to organise one event.
You might have WhatsApp for communication, Google Forms for RSVPs, spreadsheets for guest lists, bank transfers for payments, paper lists at the entrance, and another platform if tickets are involved,” said Yusuf.
“It works, but it creates a lot of manual work and friction for the organiser. A lot of event platforms also focus mainly on public ticketed events. We wanted SecVite to work just as well for a private wedding or birthday where you may need guest approvals, invitations, contributions and controlled access.”
The self-funded startup now has over 600 users, and is thinking about raising pre-seed investment to help it grow.
“A lot of our first users came through my wedding, so they originally experienced SecVite as guests rather than organisers,” said Yusuf. “The next stage for us has been getting more people to actually use the platform to run their own events.”
SecVite has started onboarding other organisers and supporting external events as well.
“That has actually been very useful because we are learning things that you don’t always discover while building the product,” said Yusuf. “Right now, I care more about seeing organisers use SecVite repeatedly for real events than just trying to grow the user number as quickly as possible.”
SecVite is focused on weddings, birthdays, private celebrations and other events where managing guests and running the event day can quickly become stressful.
“Longer-term, we see SecVite expanding across Africa because a lot of the problems we are solving are not unique to Nigeria. But I don’t want us to rush into too many countries. The priority is getting the product and business model right in Nigeria first, then expanding from there,” Yusuf said.
Organisers can start using SecVite without paying an upfront fee, with the startup instead making money when transactions happen through an event. Depending on the transaction, SecVite charges a service fee of between five and 7.5 per cent.
“This can include ticket purchases, cash gifts and contributions, vendor payments and our digital Money Spray feature,” Yusuf said. “We are still very early, so we don’t have meaningful revenue or profit yet. At this stage, We are more focused on proving that organisers will keep using SecVite and that guests will actually transact through the platform. Once we prove that consistently, the revenue side becomes much easier to scale.”

articles.title: Cuatro Samsung Odyssey para elegir según cómo juguemos: 49 pulgadas, OLED 4K, pantalla curva y hasta 1.100 Hz
articles.text:
Gamescom no es solo el lugar donde descubrimos los juegos que ocuparán nuestras próximas horas frente a la pantalla. En Colonia también estamos viendo el hardware que quiere acompañarlos, desde una Xbox Series X25 que nuestro compañero Alejandro Alcolea ya ha podido ver en directo hasta la nueva generación de monitores que Samsung ha llevado a la feria. La compañía ha presentado allí su gama Odyssey 2027 con cuatro propuestas que parten de una misma pregunta: qué debería priorizar nuestra pantalla cuando lo que cambia es, precisamente, nuestra forma de jugar.
Odyssey OLED G9: jugar a lo ancho
El primero de esos caminos pasa por ir a lo grande, literalmente. El Odyssey OLED G9 apuesta por un panel de 49 pulgadas en formato ultrapanorámico y resolución Dual QHD de 5120 × 1440 píxeles, una combinación pensada para ampliar el campo de visión sin renunciar a una frecuencia elevada. Samsung lo presenta como el primer monitor gaming DQHD de este tamaño capaz de alcanzar 360 Hz, aunque mediante Dual Mode también permite bajar a 2560 × 720 píxeles para subir hasta 720 Hz.
Por debajo de ese formato, Samsung incorpora un panel QD-OLED de quinta generación con tecnología Penta Tandem, una estructura de cinco capas que, según la compañía, es hasta 1,3 veces más eficiente y ofrece hasta el doble de vida útil que la generación anterior. También adopta una disposición de subpíxeles RGB Stripe para reducir los contornos de color y favorecer una mayor nitidez del texto. El conjunto se completa con un tiempo de respuesta GtG de 0,03 ms y un brillo máximo declarado de hasta 1.300 nits en una ventana del 3%.
Odyssey OLED G8: resolución o velocidad
El OLED G8 cambia de enfoque y apuesta por darnos margen para elegir qué queremos priorizar en cada partida. Su panel de 32 pulgadas puede trabajar en resolución UHD a 360 Hz, bajar a QHD para alcanzar 520 Hz o quedarse en Full HD y subir hasta 680 Hz. Ese Triple Mode permite adaptar el monitor tanto al tipo de juego como al rendimiento que pueda ofrecer nuestro equipo: mantener el 4K cuando buscamos más detalle o reducir resolución cuando la velocidad pasa a ocupar el primer plano.
En el resto de la ficha técnica encontramos varias tecnologías que ya hemos visto en el G9, incluido el QD-OLED de quinta generación con Penta Tandem y disposición RGB Stripe. Aquí Samsung añade Glare Free para reducir los reflejos y un tiempo de respuesta GtG de 0,03 ms, además de anunciar DisplayHDR True Black 600, AMD FreeSync Premium Pro y NVIDIA G-SYNC Compatible. La conectividad es especialmente completa: DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20, dos HDMI, USB-C con 98 W de Power Delivery, dos puertos USB de bajada y KVM integrado.
Odyssey OLED G7: 42 pulgadas y curva
El OLED G7 se aleja de la carrera por las frecuencias extremas para centrarse en otra forma de jugar: una pantalla grande y envolvente. Sus 42 pulgadas mantienen un formato 16:9, pero adoptan una curvatura 1000R que acerca los extremos del panel a nuestro campo de visión, con resolución 4K y una tasa de refresco de 165 Hz. Samsung orienta esta combinación especialmente a RPG y mundos abiertos, donde el tamaño de la imagen y la sensación de inmersión pueden pesar más que alcanzar varios cientos de hercios.
Samsung completa esa apuesta por el gran formato con un tiempo de respuesta GtG de 0,03 ms y la tecnología Glare Free para contener los reflejos procedentes de fuentes de luz externas. La compañía señala además que la superficie útil de estas 42 pulgadas es aproximadamente un 72% mayor que la del modelo anterior de 32 pulgadas que utiliza como referencia, una comparación que ayuda a entender el salto de escala. También lo presenta como el primer monitor gaming OLED curvo de 42 pulgadas con relación de aspecto 16:9 del mundo.
Odyssey G6: la carrera hacia 1.100 Hz
El G6 lleva la búsqueda de velocidad mucho más lejos y, de paso, cambia el OLED por un panel Fast IPS de 27 pulgadas. Está pensado para juegos competitivos y especialmente para FPS, con un Dual Mode que permite escoger entre QHD a 600 Hz o resolución HD a nada menos que 1.100 Hz. Alcanzar esa cifra implica renunciar a definición, pero abre la puerta a maximizar la fluidez cuando cada fotograma cuenta. Samsung lo presenta como el primer monitor gaming de 1.100 Hz del mundo, aunque LG ya cuenta con el UltraGear 25G590B, capaz de alcanzar también esa frecuencia mediante overclocking desde sus 1.000 Hz nativos.
El G6 que llegará a las tiendas será incluso más rápido que el que conocimos a comienzos de año. En CES 2026, Samsung había enseñado este modelo con hasta 1.040 Hz en HD; ahora, la especificación definitiva sube hasta 1.100 Hz, mientras que el modo QHD permanece en 600 Hz. A esa frecuencia se suma un tiempo de respuesta de 1 ms. También es el único de los cuatro Odyssey para el que tenemos ya una ventana comercial concreta: su lanzamiento global está previsto para algún momento del segundo semestre de 2026.
Como hemos visto, Samsung reparte sus cuatro modelos entre tamaño, resolución, inmersión y velocidad, de modo que la elección dependerá mucho más de cómo juguemos que de buscar un ganador absoluto. Aún queda, eso sí, una pieza importante por conocer: cuánto costará cada uno. La compañía no ha anunciado precios y tampoco ha concretado por ahora la disponibilidad de todos los modelos en cada mercado.

articles.title: Rapido faces app outage as ride booking issue hit users
articles.text:
Rapido faces app outage as ride booking issue hit users
Rapido users reported booking, location and login issues amid an app outage, as the mobility platform.
Rapido, one of India’s largest one-stop mobility platforms, faced a technical disruption on August 27, with users taking to X to report issues booking rides, selecting destinations, loading addresses, and accessing parts of the app.
Downtime Detector, a real-time tracking service that monitors the operational status and availability of websites, apps, and internet services in India, showed a spike in user complaints, including reports from Delhi, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Haryana.
Complaints included location failures, login problems, and server errors. However, the service-status page simultaneously showed no cities with confirmed outages, meaning the data indicates widespread user problems but does not establish the geographic scale or technical cause of the disruption.
“Earlier today, some users experienced a brief technical issue while booking rides on the Rapido platform. Our internal teams identified and resolved the issue promptly, and all services have since been fully restored. We regret any inconvenience caused and thank our users for their continued trust and patience,” a Rapido spokesperson said when asked by YourStory for comment.
The incident comes as the mobility platform, which has been investing heavily in technology, supply and expansion, sees competition intensifying across India’s cities.
In May, the company announced $240 million in primary funding led by Prosus, as part of a larger $730 million primary and secondary financing that valued Rapido at $3 billion. The company said the fresh capital would be used to expand into high-growth markets, strengthen its captain network and invest in technology and platform efficiency.
That expansion is happening as rivals move deeper into the same markets. Uber announced in August that it was adding 100 Indian cities, taking its footprint to 225 cities, with Uber Bike leading the push into Tier-II and Tier-III markets. Uber said reliability and affordability would be important to retaining customers in these markets.
(This article has been updated with a statement from Rapido.)

articles.title: Realme lance le C100 : le smartphone d'entrée de gamme devient plus costaud
articles.text:
Auparavant, les smartphones d'entrée de gamme de Realme étaient vendus moins de 100 euros. Non exempts de petits bugs, ralentissements et d'une fluidité discutables, le constructeur lance un nouveau smartphone un peu plus musclé.
À quelques jours de la rentrée scolaire, Realme annonce son dernier modèle d'entrée de gamme, le C100. L'objectif du constructeur avec ce smartphone : conquérir les plus jeunes en proposant une autonomie XXL, mais également un tarif accessible.
Un smartphone robuste pour les jeunes
Si l'utilisation des smartphones et appareils connectés est désormais davantage encadrée dans les établissements scolaires, le smartphone peut toujours être utilisé hors des cours pour se divertir, s'occuper ou discuter. Justement, le fabricant cible les jeunes avec ce nouvel appareil, annoncé comme robuste.
Niveau conception, le Realme C100 est en effet certifié MIL-STD-810H, une norme militaire lui offrant une robustesse certaine. L'idéal pour les jeunes pas toujours attentionnés avec leur smartphone. L'appareil est certifié IP64, résistant aux éclaboussures, et dispose d'un système anti-vol dédié.
Des caractéristiques aussi solides
Le Realme C100 intègre une batterie de 6 600 mAh lui offrant une autonomie annoncée allant jusqu'à trois jours selon le fabricant. La puissance maximale de charge est de 45 watts. Sa durée de vie globale est estimée à six ans par le fabricant.
Le Realme C100 est également doté d'une dalle de 6,8 pouces avec une fréquence de 144 Hz, une première pour un smartphone de cette gamme chez Realme. Côté photo, il dispose d'un capteur principal de 50 mégapixels, et pour stocker toutes vos photos, d'une capacité de stockage extensible à 2 To via l'ajout d'une carte micro-SD. Le smartphone est compatible 5G.
Prix et disponibilité
Le realme C100 est décliné en deux coloris : Vert (Sprouting Green) et Violet (Blooming Purple). Il est commercialisé aux tarifs recommandés suivants :
- Version 128 Go : 239,99 €
- Version 256 Go : 259,99 €

articles.title: Bill Gates advierte sobre la IA: “será el mayor igualador jamás inventado o la peor fuente de injusticia”
articles.text:
El empresario y filántropo Bill Gates lanzó una advertencia sobre el futuro de la inteligencia artificial (IA) a través de su blog personal, en el que plantea que esta tecnología “será el mayor igualador jamás inventado o la peor fuente de injusticia”.
El fundador de Microsoft sostiene que la humanidad se encuentra ante una disyuntiva histórica, cuya resolución dependerá de las decisiones colectivas que se adopten en los próximos años. En su análisis, subraya la urgencia de prepararse para el impacto social, político y económico que traerá la IA y afirma que el desafío es monumental.
PUBLICIDAD
De qué forma la IA puede ser el mayor igualador o la peor fuente de injusticia
Gates considera que la inteligencia artificial puede convertirse en un instrumento de equidad sin precedentes, pero advierte: “El desafío es monumental. Incluso en las mejores circunstancias, la transición a esta nueva era de la IA será uno de los periodos más turbulentos de la historia de la humanidad”.
El empresario plantea que la clave estará en cómo se utilice la inteligencia artificial para construir un mundo más justo y evitar que se amplíe la brecha entre ricos y pobres.
PUBLICIDAD
La advertencia se fundamenta en la ausencia de planes concretos para facilitar la transición hacia la era de la IA. “No veo indicios de que los líderes, expertos y comunidades estén afrontando los desafíos adecuadamente. No existe ningún plan para facilitar la transición a la era de la IA”, sostiene Gates.
Esta falta de preparación podría traducirse en una mayor concentración de riqueza y oportunidades en pocas manos, incrementando la desigualdad.
Cuáles son los riesgos más presentes de la inteligencia artificial según Gates
El fundador de Microsoft identifica tres grandes riesgos asociados a la expansión de la IA: la destrucción de empleos, la capacidad de la tecnología para causar daño y el impacto en el desarrollo humano y las relaciones sociales.
PUBLICIDAD
“Muchos empleos desaparecerán para siempre”, advierte Gates, quien recuerda que los puestos más vulnerables serán los de nivel básico e intermedio. La transición será rápida y abarcará sectores como ventas, atención al cliente, ingeniería de software y asistencia jurídica.
Además, Gates alerta sobre el aumento de ciberdelitos, desinformación y manipulación social facilitados por la IA: “El fraude, la desinformación, las falsificaciones profundas (deepfakes) y la vigilancia facilitados por la inteligencia artificial son algunos de los perjuicios que muchas personas sentirán con mayor intensidad en su vida cotidiana”.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo la IA cambiará la educación y el desarrollo de los jóvenes
Para Gates, la inteligencia artificial puede modificar profundamente la educación y el desarrollo social. “La misma herramienta que permitirá a las personas aprender más que nunca también podría provocar que muchas aprendan menos”, sostiene.
El empresario advierte que la facilidad de interacción con sistemas de IA puede reemplazar relaciones humanas fundamentales, sobre todo en la infancia y adolescencia.
La preocupación se extiende al pensamiento crítico. “Una encuesta preliminar sugirió que un mayor uso de la IA se asociaba con un menor pensamiento crítico. El efecto fue más pronunciado en los jóvenes”, escribió Gates.
PUBLICIDAD
El riesgo radica en que la IA fomente la dependencia y reduzca la capacidad de discernir información veraz en un ecosistema saturado de desinformación y manipulación digital.
Qué oportunidades puede generar la IA para el bien común
A pesar de sus advertencias, Gates reconoce que la inteligencia artificial ofrece oportunidades inéditas para resolver problemas globales. Destaca el potencial de la IA en áreas como la salud, la agricultura y los servicios públicos.
PUBLICIDAD
“La atención médica es un área donde la IA puede ayudar a resolver problemas reales. Muchos hospitales pequeños de Estados Unidos carecen de especialistas in situ que puedan diagnosticar rápidamente a un paciente durante una emergencia potencialmente mortal”, explica el empresario.
Asimismo, Gates señala que la IA puede nivelar el acceso a conocimientos y recursos, permitiendo a individuos y pequeñas empresas competir con grandes corporaciones.
PUBLICIDAD
El empresario resalta la utilidad de la IA para personas con discapacidad, al facilitar una vida más independiente, y para gobiernos que buscan mejorar la eficiencia de los servicios sociales.

articles.title: PaperCut warns of NG, MF flaw exploited in zero-day attacks
articles.text:
PaperCut is warning that hackers are actively exploiting a vulnerability in all versions of its PaperCut NG and PaperCut MF print management software in zero-day attacks.
The company says it is aware of confirmed attacks on customers and is urging organizations with Internet-exposed PaperCut Application Servers to immediately restrict access to the web interfaces to trusted IP addresses.
"PaperCut Software security response team is investigating active exploitation of a vulnerability affecting PaperCut NG and PaperCut MF," reads an urgent security advisory published Thursday.
"We are aware of confirmed customer incidents and are treating this matter with the highest priority."
PaperCut says the vulnerability affects all versions of PaperCut NG and MF, but has not shared details about the flaw or how it is being exploited.
The company says its security team reproduced the vulnerability using information provided by a University customer.
PaperCut has now released emergency patches for customers with public-facing PaperCut NG/MF servers.
"This is an emergency patch for customers with public-facing PaperCut NG/MF servers who are unable to take other mitigating action," reads the advisory.
The company continues to warn customers whose Application Servers are exposed to the Internet to use firewall rules or network access controls to restrict their web interfaces to trusted IP addresses.
PaperCut also shared indicators of compromise that could indicate whether a server has been compromised.
These include suspicious activity from the the legitimate PaperCut pc-app.exe process and server.log files that have been modified, deleted, or are missing.
Administrators should also look for the following errors in server.log:
ERROR No suitable driver found for jdbc:no:x
ERROR DatabaseUtils - Database error looking up cardID: VALUES CAST
However, PaperCut warns that a lack of indicators does not mean that a server has not been compromised.
At this time, PaperCut has not disclosed who is behind the attacks, what attackers are doing after compromising servers, or whether data is being stolen.
PaperCut says it will continue updating its advisory with additional indicators of compromise and remediation guidance as its investigation continues.
BleepingComputer contacted PaperCut with questions about this exploitation and will update the story when we receive a response.
Previous PaperCut flaws exploited in attacks
PaperCut has a history of being targeted by threat actors after security vulnerabilities were disclosed.
In April 2023, attackers began exploiting the critical CVE-2023-27350 PaperCut vulnerability, which allowed unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and remotely execute code on vulnerable servers.
Microsoft later linked some of those attacks to the Clop ransomware operation, which exploited vulnerable PaperCut servers for initial access to company networks. Microsoft also observed intrusions that led to LockBit ransomware attacks.
While PaperCut has a Print Archiving feature that can retain documents sent through a server, Clop later told BleepingComputer that it had used the vulnerabilities for initial access to victim networks rather than to steal archived documents directly from PaperCut servers.
The exploitation spread to other threat actors, with Microsoft reporting that Iranian state-backed hacking groups were also exploiting CVE-2023-27350.
CISA and the FBI issued a joint advisory in May 2023 warning that the Bl00dy Ransomware Gang was also exploiting vulnerable PaperCut servers in attacks against the education sector.

Bravia 6 : le nouveau TV Oled 4K de Sony affiche un tarif agressif, du 48 au 83 pouces
articles.text:
Bravia 6 : le nouveau TV Oled 4K de Sony affiche un tarif agressif, du 48 au 83 pouces
Sony vient d’étoffer sa gamme de téléviseurs avec un nouveau Bravia 6. Disponible de 48 à 83 pouces, ce modèle 4K mise sur la technologie Oled, Google TV, et des prix plutôt agressifs pour la marque.
Sony continue d’étoffer son catalogue de téléviseurs après un excellent Bravia 9 II en Mini-Led RGB, et vient d’annoncer aujourd’hui le Bravia 6, un nouveau modèle Oled qui vient compléter une gamme déjà bien fournie. Le constructeur japonais mise ici sur une série plus accessible, proposée dans pas moins de cinq diagonales, de 48 à 83 pouces.
Avec un premier prix fixé à 1200 €, le Bravia 6 pourrait surtout constituer une porte d’entrée intéressante dans l’univers de l'Oled, et de Sony, généralement assez onéreux.
Une dalle Oled 4K abordable, on aime
Situé entre les Bravia 5 et Bravia 7 en Mini-Led, le Bravia 6 mise donc sur une dalle Oled 4K composée de pixels auto-émissifs. Chaque pixel pouvant produire sa propre lumière et s’éteindre indépendamment, cette technologie permet d’obtenir des noirs parfaits et un excellent niveau de contraste, comme sur l’ensemble des téléviseurs Oled.
Sony y ajoute sa technologie Triluminos Pro, chargée d’améliorer la reproduction des couleurs et d'offrir des teintes plus riches et naturelles. Le fabricant ne communique en revanche pas de chiffre concernant la luminosité de la dalle, un point qu’il faudra donc vérifier lors d’un éventuel passage dans notre laboratoire. On imagine que ce modèle embarque une dalle de chez LG Display similaire à celle du B6, Oled d’entrée de gamme de LG. Il devrait donc être un cran en dessous du LG C6 et du Samsung S92H.
Le Bravia 6 prend également en charge le Dolby Vision pour les contenus HDR. Côté son, Sony annonce une compatibilité Dolby Atmos et DTS:X, de quoi profiter des principaux formats audio immersifs du marché.
Sony Bravia 6
Google TV accueille Gemini sur le Sony Bravia 6
Pour la partie Smart TV, pas de grosse surprise puisque Sony reste fidèle à Google TV. L’interface permet évidemment d’accéder aux principales applications de streaming et profite désormais de l’intégration de Gemini.
L’intelligence artificielle de Google doit notamment permettre de rendre les interactions avec le téléviseur plus naturelles et de faciliter la recherche de contenus. Reste à voir ce que cette intégration apportera réellement au quotidien et quelles fonctions seront disponibles en français au lancement.
Des prix agressifs pour un téléviseur Sony
C’est du côté des tarifs que le Bravia 6 se montre assez intéressant. Sony nous a habitués à des tarifs élevés sur ses téléviseurs, mais celui-ci reste relativement abordable avec des tarifs similaires à ce que l’on trouve chez LG sur le B6 ou Samsung sur les S85H. Sony proposera cinq diagonales et le prix ne grimpe finalement pas tant que cela lorsqu’on passe aux très grandes tailles :
- 48 pouces : 1199 €
- 55 pouces : 1299 €
- 65 pouces : 1799 €
- 77 pouces : 2499 €
- 83 pouces : 2999 €
Sony n’a malheureusement pas précisé la date exacte de disponibilité des différentes diagonales. Il faudra également attendre nos mesures pour savoir ce que vaut réellement cette nouvelle série en matière de luminosité, de fidélité des couleurs et de traitement d’image !

articles.title: The Ugandan founders who don’t want farmers waiting for rain
articles.text:
Rodgers Mwijukye and Ronald Asiimwe have known each other long enough to disagree without making much of it. They met in high school in Uganda in 2015, attended the same university, and took degrees that pointed towards very different careers. Mwijukye studied water and irrigation engineering; Asiimwe studied computer science.
Mwijukye imagined postgraduate study, perhaps a PhD and a career in academia or public service. Asiimwe was the software guy, happiest behind a computer. Agriculture, however, kept pulling them towards the same problem.
In Uganda, millions of farmers still depend on rainfall to grow food. For farmers in drought-prone areas, a failed rainy season can mean a failed harvest and, with it, the loss of a household’s income and food. Mwijukye had trained in precisely the engineering that could help farmers become less dependent on rain.
The duo founded Drought Guard Africa in 2023, which designs and installs climate-smart irrigation, clean water, and solar energy systems for rural farmers, refugee settlements, and underserved communities.
But building the technology turned out to be easier than persuading farmers to trust it. Many had farmed the same way for generations. A new irrigation system, however clever, meant little until they could see it working on someone else’s farm.
“People believe successful stories from the people they know,” Mwijukye says.
It is a lesson that captures much of their journey. Africa may have the technology, but the harder problem is getting it onto farms where it can actually change how food is grown.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
If the two of you had never met, where do you think your lives would have ended up?
Mwijukye: I think I would probably be in public service or have continued with education. I did a bachelor’s degree in water and irrigation engineering, and I always felt I could go for a master’s, then a PhD, and perhaps join academia. Or I could have ended up working in public service in the water and irrigation space.
Asiimwe: I don’t know why he’s saying this because the truth is, he founded this before I joined him. He didn’t get into it because we were together.
We’ve been together for more than 10 years. We met in high school in 2015 and went up to Senior Six together. We later took different paths but ended up at the same university. I was doing computer science, but I would always go to his room.
If we had never met, I think I would still have ended up in agriculture. Most of the projects I worked on at university were agriculture-related. Before this, we also co-founded a youth NGO. I’m still part of it, although I don’t put much time into it anymore because most of my focus is here.
When did you first realise your co-founder wasn’t just a good colleague, but someone you’d trust with your career—and perhaps your reputation?
Mwijukye: For me, it goes back to when we met in high school in 2015. We literally shared almost everything. From 2015 until around 2021, it was simply a friendship. We were always together, so we knew each other very well and trusted each other with almost everything.
That made it easier for me to share the vision with him. It didn’t take him long to say, “Yeah, we can do this.”
Asiimwe: After 11 years, he’s like a brother to me. Even without the business, we would still be close. I can stay in his room, and we can share almost everything. Business isn’t what brought us together in the first place. It’s almost a complement to the friendship.
What’s something about your co-founder that frustrated you in the beginning but has since become one of the company’s biggest strengths?
Mwijukye: When it comes to finding potential investors, grants, or other opportunities, that is not his thing. I would tell him, “Look, you can use LinkedIn for most of these things. People are always sharing opportunities. You just have to make yourself available and keep looking.”
Even when I found an opportunity, following up and doing the application wasn’t his game. He’s into tech. He loves being on his computer coding.
Eventually, I realised that it was actually useful because our roles became clear. I knew he could do that, so I had to do this. If I spend a day without scrolling through LinkedIn and different groups looking for opportunities, I feel like I’ve lost a million. I find the opportunities that fit us and do the applications.
Asiimwe: For me, it’s his decision-making. Sometimes he comes across as a dictator. I tend to look at things objectively and ask, “How do you feel about this?” On his side, sometimes it’s just, “Let’s do this.”
But I’ve realised that when he strongly believes in something, he puts all his energy behind it. What he speaks about, he enforces and supports. That has become a strength for the business.
You’ve spent years trying to solve other people’s problems. Who helped you solve yours when you were close to giving up?
Asiimwe: We’re solving farmers’ problems, although we also benefit because that’s how the business makes revenue.
Along my journey, I’ve had many people helping me. Growing up, my family wasn’t really middle-class. Getting into a good school and university was difficult. But I grew up with scholarships. I got through high school on a scholarship and university through a government scholarship.
So I feel like other people were solving my problems. That’s partly where I get the heart to help solve other people’s problems. Now I can combine that passion with business.
Mwijukye: My elder brother has been very important. He works in cold storage, and he helped give me the belief that there is enough money in the world and investors are willing to fund you if you identify a real problem and organise yourself properly to solve it.
At the beginning, we didn’t have enough money to run the business. That period is difficult because without support, you can easily crash and start thinking, “Maybe this isn’t meant for me.” My brother kept encouraging me. Where financial support was required, he put some money in because he understood the vision and believed in the idea.
Every founder has one decision they’d reverse if they could. What’s yours?
Asiimwe: Hiring friends. We’ve had people on the team who later became problematic. There’s one person, for example, whom I felt wasn’t doing things genuinely and sometimes cheated the company. But he was our friend.
Hiring friends can make running a business harder because it becomes difficult to remove them when things aren’t working. If we could reverse that decision, we probably wouldn’t have hired him in the first place.
Mwijukye: I agree. Friendship really complicates business when somebody isn’t doing what they’re supposed to do. Because you’re close friends, it becomes much harder to deal with the problem purely as a business issue.
If you swapped roles tomorrow, which one of you would struggle more—and why?
Asiimwe: I would struggle more. From this conversation, you can probably already tell that most of those decisions come from him, and he’s really good at them.
Mwijukye: He also hasn’t attended many of these conferences and summits. He loves being on his computer coding.
Asiimwe: But from experience, I think I would cope. Our roles overlap sometimes. When he isn’t around, I play some of his roles, and he does the same with mine.
You’re both in the business of hope. What’s the most hopeless you’ve felt since starting the company?
Mwijukye: For me, it was around the beginning of 2024. We had significant demand from farmers who wanted new systems, but the revenue from our existing farmers wasn’t enough to finance the supply. We tried looking for external funding from banks, but we couldn’t get it because they required documentation and assets that we didn’t have.
It was a really difficult period. You start asking yourself, “Why did I even start this?” We eventually reached out to my brother, who injected a loan into the business. That helped us cover the gap until we received some grant funding.
Asiimwe: For me, it was 2023 when we first started. It didn’t really make sense where we were going because we had almost no capital. What we had couldn’t do the things we were aspiring to do. I kept wondering, “Are we really doing the right thing? Am I just wasting another year?”
Mwijukye: When you’re starting, everything looks good on paper. You think, “Yes, this solution is going to work miracles.” But you haven’t tested whether the communities will actually adopt it.
These are people who have relied on rain-fed agriculture all their lives. You arrive and tell them, “This can transform your farming. You don’t have to rely on rain.” They aren’t immediately going to believe you.
You have to train people. You need demonstration sites. Sometimes you need local government officials or extension officers to come with you. You install an irrigation system and let people see that it works for somebody they know. People believe success stories from people they trust. That was one of the hardest lessons at the beginning.
Outside boardrooms and investor meetings, what do you enjoy talking about that has absolutely nothing to do with startups or climate?
Mwijukye: Football. I’m a Manchester United supporter.
I’m also someone who doesn’t enjoy being in places with lots of people. I enjoy being alone. On a weekend, as long as I have internet, electricity, and my TV, I can spend the entire weekend watching Manchester United—and hate-watching other teams. Before you realise it, the day is gone. That’s basically my life outside work.
Asiimwe: My hobbies are more hands-on. I don’t really like watching; I prefer participating. If it’s football, I play. I also play basketball and indoor games.
When people hear “Africa’s future”, they usually speak about technology. Are we becoming too obsessed with innovation and not obsessed enough with execution?
Asiimwe: That’s very true. Look at Uganda and compare it with countries that developed decades ago. They didn’t have the AI we’re talking about today, yet hunger wasn’t the problem it remains in parts of Africa. It’s 2026. We’re talking about AI and entering a robotic era, yet people in Karamoja are dying of hunger.
So are we really solving the problem? The underlying problem isn’t necessarily that we haven’t adopted enough technology. Maybe we simply aren’t doing the work. We have land that isn’t being used. Or where we are using it, perhaps we aren’t using it properly. Technology isn’t necessarily what has kept us behind.
Mwijukye: I agree. Technology is not Africa’s biggest problem. Execution is. Even without today’s technology, people can solve many of these problems. Our ancestors had problems with food and housing, too, and they had to innovate. Somebody found a way to preserve food. Somebody worked out how to make fire from stones. We need technology, yes, but technology alone cannot solve everything.
Asiimwe: How, in 2026, does Africa still have hunger? How is that possible? We have all this technology and plenty of land, including huge amounts of unused and underutilised land.
What’s one compliment you’ve received that meant far more than any award or funding announcement?
Asiimwe: People say I’m reliable. Once I promise something, I really try to deliver because I like keeping my word. When somebody says I’m reliable, I appreciate that they can see it.
Mwijukye: Trustworthy. I can keep secrets.
Suppose someone gave you $100 million today with one condition: you couldn’t spend it on Drought Guard Africa. What problem would you dedicate your life to instead?
Mwijukye: I would probably solve a similar problem. Take Karamoja in northern Uganda. People are dying because of hunger, yet Karamoja has land that can be farmed. The solution cannot simply be continually taking food there.
If you want to teach your children how to feed themselves, you don’t just keep bringing them food. You show them how food is produced. If I had that money, I would go to Karamoja and establish something that enables people there to farm for themselves. The people themselves would have to be at the centre of it.
Asiimwe: With the experience I have now, I would probably use the same model we already know. It’s incredibly hard to start a completely different business from scratch, even when you have money. I’m a software guy, and I’ve thought about businesses like importing things from China or writing software.
But now I know that the model we have works. I know the pipeline and understand the ecosystem. So if I couldn’t invest in Drought Guard Africa, I would probably start something different that solves a very similar problem.
What’s something you’ve become less certain about as you’ve grown older?
Asiimwe: I’ve learned not to depend on government support. When we started, we thought we might get support from local government officials or government grants. As we operated, we realised that it shouldn’t be our focus.
The Ugandan government does provide money, but accessing it can be difficult. So we’ve grown to understand that we shouldn’t rely on those things. We need to make our own money and use that money to make more money.
Mwijukye: For me, it’s trusting people. People change. When you’re younger, you think, “This is my friend. I can share everything with this person,” or you assume somebody will come and help you. Then you grow up and realise everyone has their own problems. You have to wake up and do the work. You can’t sit there waiting for somebody.
Asiimwe: I’ve also become less certain about employee loyalty. A lot of people care more about the money they are getting than the vision.
There are people on the team who genuinely support the idea and the vision. But you can’t simply assume loyalty. If you give the wrong person too much power, they can cheat the customer or cheat the company.
If I asked your closest friends whether success has changed you, what would they say?
Asiimwe: They would probably say it hasn’t. But success is supposed to change some things. If you get money, maybe you won’t wear the same clothes or go to the same places anymore.
Mwijukye: I don’t completely agree. There’s a saying that when a blind man regains his sight, the first thing he throws away is the walking stick that helped him. Sometimes you don’t notice how you’ve changed. Maybe your friends have certain cars, clothes, or shoes, and when you finally have enough money, you start buying those things too.
But people will always interpret your decisions differently. Someone might want you to go out with them on the weekend, but you have an application due on Monday. You decide to stay home and finish it because that application could bring revenue into your business. That friend may simply say, “Since he got money, he doesn’t visit us anymore.”
Asiimwe: I think what changes is what people see from the outside. Maybe I used to stay in a two-star hotel, and now I stay in a five-star hotel. That’s a lifestyle change. What matters is whether my values—integrity, honesty, and the things I believe in—have changed.
You’re building a company on a continent that often rewards patience less than speed. Have you ever felt pressure to pretend the business was doing better than it actually was?
Asiimwe: It happens. We did some of that at the beginning because the pressure was intense. That was around 2023. But we didn’t continue doing it. We had a friend who was around the team then, and he had mastered the language of exaggeration. He could talk about very big things that we hadn’t actually achieved yet. He would brag about them.
That has never really been my thing. Bragging about things you haven’t achieved doesn’t help because when you lie to other people, you also lie to yourself. Eventually, your brain starts thinking you have already achieved those things, and you stop putting in the work.
Sometimes you meet someone years later and think, “You used to talk about all these big things. What happened?” That’s the danger. Talking big can give you hope, but it can also convince you that you’ve already done the work when you haven’t.
Describe each other using just one word. Then explain why.
Mwijukye: Genius.
Asiimwe: Visionary.
Twenty years from now, when your children or grandchildren ask, “What were you trying to fix?” what answer would make you most proud?
Mwijukye: Maybe 20 years from now, technology will have advanced so much that hunger will no longer be a problem. Our children might struggle to understand what people were going through during our time.
I would tell them about what farmers in northeastern Uganda went through: the droughts, climate change, and the difficulty of producing food. I would tell them about the pain farmers experienced and how we tried to solve some of those problems through irrigation systems and the technologies we implemented. Hopefully, it will sound strange to them, like the stories we hear today about what life was like before phones.
Asiimwe: For me, the story would be about food security. I would tell them how people once died of hunger on one of the most fertile continents in the world, and how little had been done to support the systems that could prevent that. And I would tell them that we tried to change that.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: 2 heures par jour sur Facebook et Instagram : Meta s'engage à limiter l'accès des mineurs aux États-Unis
articles.text:
C’est un procès historique qui vient de se terminer devant un tribunal d’Oakland (Californie). Vingt-neuf États américains accusaient Meta d’avoir nui à la santé mentale des mineurs. L’entreprise de Mark Zuckerberg a notamment été accusée d’avoir mis en place les comptes adolescents tout en sachant que certaines des limites qui y sont imposées pouvaient être contournées ou ne pas être suffisamment efficaces. Face aux diverses accusations, Meta a annoncé plusieurs mesures pour mieux protéger les plus jeunes et proposé un accord pouvant atteindre 17,1 milliards de dollars pour mettre un terme aux poursuites.
Des limites imposées aux adolescents américains
Meta s’est engagé à mettre en place une série de mesures pour mieux protéger les jeunes américains. D’une part, les moins de 18 ans auront accès à Instagram et Facebook durant deux heures cumulées par jour. D’autre part, les notifications seront fortement limitées. Durant la nuit, de 22 heures à 7 heures du matin, elles seront totalement coupées. Durant les heures de classe, de 8 heures à 15 heures, les notifications seront également coupées pour les mineurs. Notons également deux points : les compteurs de mentions « j’aime » seront automatiquement masqués et les filtres relatifs à la chirurgie esthétique désactivés.
Ces limitations entreront en vigueur au sein de la cinquantaine d’États signataires dans les six mois. Un parent, dont le compte est lié à celui de l’adolescent, pourra toutefois assouplir ces restrictions. Notons enfin que la plateforme de messagerie WhatsApp, appartenant à Meta, n’est quant à elle pas concernée par ces mesures restrictives.
Meta va payer jusqu’à 17,1 milliards de dollars pour mettre un terme aux poursuites
Meta s’est engagé auprès de 47 États américains à payer jusqu’à 17,1 milliards de dollars (environ 14,7 milliards d’euros) dans le cadre d’un accord visant à mettre un terme aux poursuites concernant la protection des mineurs. Ce paiement pourra être échelonné sur dix ans et les États qui percevront cet argent l’investiront notamment dans des mesures et des structures destinées à protéger les plus jeunes.
Point important : cet accord ne met en aucun cas un terme aux diverses poursuites dont fait actuellement l’objet Meta. Il s’agit seulement du dénouement de l’un des nombreux procès actuellement en cours contre l’entreprise. Quoi qu’il en soit, la question de l’utilisation des réseaux sociaux devient de plus en plus un sujet de santé publique. Si cela fait maintenant plusieurs années que des organismes et collectifs tirent la sonnette d’alarme, des mesures concrètes sont maintenant prises pour protéger les plus jeunes. Le Royaume-Uni, la France ou encore le Vietnam ont chacun annoncé un plan visant à interdire les réseaux sociaux aux plus jeunes. De leur côté, une cinquantaine d’États américains viennent donc de faire plier Meta avec la mise en place de mesures concrètes.
